v.why: When the cell already has convs on the internal path, swapping the residual skip on edge 3 for another conv removes a useful shortcut, whereas in conv-free cells it adds the only learnable op (exp 72,76 vs 71,73,74).
If edge 5 is a parameter-free pool, adding a conv on edge 4 provides much-needed learnable capacity on the output, giving large gains (exp 61-65 vs 20-23).
A residual skip on edge 3 helps deep conv cells but is harmful in parameter-free skip/pool cells where it replaces or dilutes the only signal (exp 7-10 vs 11-13).
With edge 1 absent, removing edge 0 cuts all input flow into intermediate nodes, collapsing paths through edges 4/5 (exp 18,19 vs 14-17).
When edge 4 is absent, removing edge 5 leaves only edge 3 (or nothing) feeding the output, causing severe degradation (exp 99 vs 98).
With edge 4 absent, edge 3 is a critical output path, so removing it is catastrophic (exp 39,40 vs 38,41).
Replacing a 3x3 conv with a 1x1 loses receptive field, while replacing skip/pool/none with 1x1 adds capacity (exp 54 vs 55-57).
When edge 0 carries a 3x3 conv, edge 4 transports that learned node-1 feature to the output, so removing it hurts more than when node 1 holds a cheap op (exp 77,81 vs 78-80).
Without the edge-3 residual, a smoothing pool on edge 5 stabilizes an all-conv cell, while with a residual present swapping a conv for pooling just loses capacity (exp 97 vs 32,35).
In pooling-dominated cells, a skip on edge 3 bypasses the remaining processing or replaces the only conv, severely hurting accuracy (exp 12,13 vs 7-10,86).
